Algebra I · Lesson 1.1

Numbers and Their Families

Solve this lesson, free →All lessons

Welcome to algebra, the study of what numbers can do. Before putting numbers to work it helps to know what they are, so this first lesson sorts them into families. The sorting itself is easy once you know the value of each number. The catch is that one number can be written in many different ways, so how a number looks is a poor guide to what it is.

Problem
Here are six numbers. 81,357,4.0,−124,0.75,1081​,735​,4.0,4−12​,0.75,10​ How many of them are integers, the numbers …,−2,−1,0,1,2,……,−2,−1,0,1,2,…?
Show a hint
  • Evaluate each number before you judge it. Some of these are not what they look like.
Show the full solution
81=981​=9, 357=5735​=5, 4.0=44.0=4, and −124=−34−12​=−3, so those four are integers. Only 0.750.75 and 1010​ miss a whole value, giving 44​. A number's family comes from its value, not from how it happens to be written.
Key idea
The integers are the counting numbers 1,2,3,…1,2,3,…, their negatives −1,−2,−3,…−1,−2,−3,…, and zero. In order they continue without end in both directions, …,−3,−2,−1,0,1,2,3,……,−3,−2,−1,0,1,2,3,…. Membership depends on value, not notation, so evaluate a number before you classify it. The value of 8181​ is 99, and 99 is an integer.
Problem
Call a number nonnegative when it is not negative, and nonpositive when it is not positive. Exactly one integer manages to be both at once. Which integer?
Show a hint
  • Nonnegative rules out one sign. Nonpositive rules out the other. What is left?
Show the full solution
Nonnegative rules out being negative, and nonpositive rules out being positive, so a number that is both must be neither, and every other number falls on one side or the other. The only one left is 00​.
Key idea
Positive means greater than zero, negative means less than zero, and zero itself is neither positive nor negative. Nonnegative means zero or positive, and nonpositive means zero or negative. Algebra needs those last two words because many quantities can equal zero but are never less than zero. A square is one example, since no square is negative.
Problem
A ratio is one integer divided by a nonzero integer. The number 88 has no fraction bar written on it, yet it is a ratio in many different ways. Write 88 as a ratio with denominator 2525. What numerator do you need?
Show a hint
  • The fraction must collapse back to 88 when you divide.
Show the full solution
20025=825200​=8, so the numerator is 200200​. Nothing about 2525 was special. The same 88 is also 8118​ and 162216​, so an integer passes the ratio test in infinitely many ways.
Key idea
A rational number is any number that can be written as one integer divided by a nonzero integer. The name comes from the word ratio. Every integer is rational, since nn equals n11n​. The denominator must be nonzero because division by zero does not produce a number.
Problem
The decimal 0.272727…0.272727… repeats the block 2727 forever. It never ends, yet it is still a ratio of integers with denominator 1111. Find the numerator.
Show a hint
  • A two-digit block repeating forever is that block over 9999. Then reduce.
Show the full solution
A repeating two-digit block sits over 9999, so 0.272727…=27990.272727…=9927​. Dividing top and bottom by 99 leaves 311113​, so the numerator is 33​. A decimal can run forever and still be a ratio of integers, as long as it repeats.
Problem
The decimal of any ratio of integers either stops or falls into a block that repeats forever. Now build 0.31311311131111…0.31311311131111… where each 33 is followed by one more 11 than the last. Does this decimal ever settle into a block that repeats forever, yes or no?
Show a hint
  • A repeating block has a fixed length. Watch what the growing runs of 1s do to any fixed length.
Show the full solution
A repeating block has some fixed length, but the runs of 11s grow past any fixed length eventually. So the block would have to be all 11s, and the 33s that keep arriving rule that out. The answer is nono​. This decimal neither stops nor repeats, so no ratio of integers equals it, and it falls outside every family met so far.
Key idea
Numbers like that are irrational. Their decimals never stop and never repeat, which is the same as saying no ratio of integers equals them. The best known examples are 22​ and ππ. A radical sign alone does not make a number irrational, since 9=39​=3 is an integer. Evaluate a root before you classify it. The square root of a whole number is either a whole number or irrational, never a fraction in between. This course proves that later.
Problem
How many of these four numbers are irrational? π2275169π722​5​169​
Show a hint
  • 227722​ is famous for approximating something irrational. What is it, itself?
  • Evaluate 169169​ before you judge it.
Show the full solution
227722​ approximates ππ, but it is an integer over a nonzero integer, rational no matter what it approximates, and 169=13169​=13, an integer. That leaves ππ and 55​ as the irrationals, and the count is 22​.
Key idea
The real numbers are all the numbers that can be written as decimals, ending or not, repeating or not. Together they fill the entire number line. The families are nested. Every integer is rational, every rational is real, and the irrational numbers are the reals that are not rational. The nesting works in one direction. An integer is automatically rational and real, but a real number need not be either.
Problem
The positive integers have a smallest member, the number 11. Is there a smallest positive rational number, yes or no?
Show a hint
  • Whatever positive rational a challenger names, cut it in half. What do you get?
Show the full solution
Half of any positive rational is smaller, still positive, and still a ratio of integers, so every candidate for smallest is beaten by its own half. No candidate can be the smallest, and the answer is nono​.
Fun fact
In 1545 Girolamo Cardano hit square roots of negative numbers in a puzzle about splitting 1010, called them useless, and computed with them anyway. They live outside the reals, and in Chapter 11 the family tree grows again to hold them.

Practice these ideas

Practice
Count the nonpositive integers that are strictly greater than −5.5−5.5, every single one of them. How many do you find?
Show the solution
The nonpositive integers greater than −5.5−5.5 are −5,−4,−3,−2,−1,0−5,−4,−3,−2,−1,0, so there are 66​. Zero counts, since nonpositive means zero or negative.
Practice
The number −561414−56​ fits at least one of the three family names integer, rational, and real. Which name is the most exclusive one that fits?
Show the solution
−5614=−414−56​=−4, an integer. Every integer is automatically rational and real, so the tightest label is integerinteger​.
Practice
The decimal 0.580.58 stops after two digits, so it is really a ratio of integers. Written in lowest terms, that ratio has what denominator?
Show the solution
0.58=581000.58=10058​, and dividing top and bottom by 22 gives 29505029​, which no longer reduces. The denominator is 5050​.
Practice
The decimal 0.2‾=0.222…0.2=0.222… repeats a single digit forever. Write it as a fraction in lowest terms.
Show the solution
Since 0.111…=190.111…=91​, doubling both sides gives 0.222…=290.222…=92​, already in lowest terms. The fraction is 2992​​.
Practice
The number 225225​ is written with a radical sign. Evaluate it and classify it, rational or irrational?
Show the solution
152=225152=225, so 225=15225​=15, an integer, and every integer is rational. The answer is rationalrational​. A radical sign does not make a number irrational, so evaluate a root before classifying it.
Practice
Every integer is rational, that street runs one way for sure. Does it run both ways, is every rational number an integer, yes or no?
Show the solution
3883​ is rational and sits strictly between 00 and 11, so it is no integer. The nesting works inward to outward only, and the answer is nono​.
Practice
Find the number sitting exactly halfway between 2552​ and 3553​ on the number line. Answer as a fraction in lowest terms.
Show the solution
Add the two and halve. 25+35=152​+53​=1, and half of 11 is 1221​​. Between any two rationals you can always find another one, the same crowding that made a smallest positive rational impossible.
Practice
The number 77​ is irrational, its decimal never stops and never repeats. Is the product 7×77​×7​ rational, yes or no?
Show the solution
By definition 77​ squares to exactly 77, and 77 is an integer, so the product is rational, yesyes​. Two irrational numbers can multiply to a rational one.
